added_claim_errors: "The 15-year clock restarts for the new beneficiary" presents an unresolved question as settled.
"This compresses to four or five years" is unsupported: future limits are unannounced, and even $8,000 × 4 = $32,000 falls short.
"The money needs to land ... by December 31, 2026" is wrong as a federal deadline; April 15, 2027 is available for a 2026 designation, subject to provider processing.
"Scholarships ... don't count" is too broad: qualifying taxable scholarship or fellowship compensation can count. Checked [IRS Publication 970](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p970).
"Most [plans] do by 2026, but not all" adds an unverified claim about adoption across plans.
"This is the most commonly missed cost" adds an unsupported ranking of state-tax mistakes.
"With distribution code 1 in Box 7" implies required reporting; code 1 is appropriate, but Box 7 codes are optional. Checked [IRS Form 1099-Q instructions](https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i1099q).
"Roll over the smallest of these three numbers" omits subtracting other IRA contributions. Step 8 partially repairs this for Roth contributions, but never addresses traditional IRA contributions.
"Limits may rise with inflation, which would shorten the schedule" is unsupported as a reduction in tax years; even $8,000 × 4 = $32,000 still requires a fifth year.

"Complete the transfer by December 31, 2026 to count against the 2026 limit" is wrong as a federal deadline; a 2026-designated rollover can occur through April 15, 2027, subject to provider processing.
"Scholarships do not [count]" is too broad: qualifying taxable scholarship or fellowship compensation can count. Checked [IRS Publication 970](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p970).
"K-12 tuition (up to $10,000 a year)" is outdated for 2026; the federal annual limit is $20,000. Checked [Washington's official 529 FAQ](https://529invest.wa.gov/resources/faq/).
"The plan can tell you the balance from five years ago" suggests an inadequate eligibility measure: qualifying current earnings must also be included.
"Some plans take two to four weeks" supplies a processing estimate without identifying a plan or substantiating that range.

reasons: Both immediately reject the $48,000 rollover and correctly identify the principal dollar caps, direct-transfer requirement, and state-tax caveat; their displayed schedule sums and $13,000 remainder arithmetic check out. Both incorrectly impose a December federal deadline, speculate about shortening the five-year schedule, and omit the excess-rollover calculation and its separate Roth and 529 consequences. B wins narrowly because it is substantially less repetitive and avoids A's categorical beneficiary-change reset claim. B still needs correction of its incomplete contribution-room formula and outdated K-12 limit.
